title: Observing the Mind and Removing Habitual Tendencies
excerpt: Excerpted from Xu Hengzhi's *What It Means to Learn Buddhism* and *How to Practice the Buddhadharma*

inline.s: Excerpted
from Xu Hengzhi's *What It Means to Learn Buddhism* and *How to Practice the Buddhadharma*
(Excerpted from *What It Means to Learn Buddhism*)

The purpose of learning Buddhism is to gain liberation from the suffering of birth and death; and to gain liberation from the suffering of birth and death, one must first illumine the mind and see one's true nature; and the essential practice for seeing the nature must begin with observing the mind. Just as, to fell a tree, one must sever its root, and, to cure an ailment by moxibustion, one must find the vital point. Therefore the *Sūtra on Contemplation of the Mind Ground* says: “You ordinary beings, because you do not observe your own mind, drift about in the sea of birth and death.” It also says: “One who can observe the mind attains ultimate liberation; one who cannot observe it remains forever entangled.”

The method of observing the mind: first let go of all the myriad entanglements, and give no thought to good deeds or bad, to past or future. Directly turn inward and observe your present thought. At this point you will only see thoughts surging back and forth, arising and ceasing without pause. Do not cling to them, do not follow after them, and do not deliberately try to dispel them; simply watch them quietly and attentively (to observe is to watch). When a deluded thought arises, one look and it vanishes without trace, but before long it arises again — simply keep watching it the same way. When no thought arises, still keep watching (this very watching is the illumination of wisdom). After long practice, once it ripens, when you see that not a single thought arises, you will realize the state of empty purity. At this moment everything before your eyes is objective reality (direct perception): clear and distinct, not without seeing and hearing (not empty), yet perfectly still, without a single thought (not existent). This very scene is the original face of your true nature (note: at this moment not even these words and phrases exist). What matters is to recognize it thoroughly, to hold it firmly, and to remain always in accord with this reality — this is what is called seeing the nature (from which it is clear that illumining the mind and seeing the nature is a natural matter, an ordinary matter, with nothing extraordinary about it at all). After seeing the nature, all delusion, karma, and suffering will naturally find a way to dissolve little by little, for once the eye of wisdom is opened, it illuminates and knows that delusion and karma are all born of the confluence of causes and conditions, and are by nature empty; when the mind no longer dwells or clings, deluded thoughts lose their footing. If one constantly practices in this way, it is called “prajñāpāramitā” (wisdom that reaches the other shore).

The method of observing the mind described above is not, in itself, restricted to any particular time: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must remain alert at all times and never for a moment depart from mindful contemplation — only then can one succeed. Nowhere under heaven is there a bargain to be had without labor, still less in learning Buddhism so as to put an end to birth and death. A beginner should practice this contemplation at least several dozen times a day, so that it may gradually ripen.

If you find your thoughts flying about and can hardly get a grip on them, then you must make use of the method of sitting meditation. When sitting, place the right foot on the left thigh — this is called the half-lotus posture; the full lotus is even better if you can manage it. The body must be held upright, unmoving and unshaken. The hands form the meditation mudrā: both palms turned upward, the right resting on the left, the two thumbs lightly touching, placed upon the crossed legs below the navel. Close the eyes to shut out light, close the mouth, press the tongue against the upper palate, and let the breath follow its own natural course. Loosen the clothing and belt, and sit in a composed, serene manner. Do not sit where there is a draft, and in the cold of autumn and winter the legs must be well covered. When the sitting is done, rub the two hands together until warm and massage the face and eyes to promote the circulation, and then rise from the seat. In this way sit quietly for at least half an hour to an hour every day — the more and the longer, the better. While seated, quietly observe and illuminate, training step by step; when the practice ripens, you will be able to observe the mind at all times, in all places, and in all things.

The stronger the power of observation, the fuller the power of concentration; concentration and wisdom nourish each other, and the deluded mind ceases of itself. Where the deluded mind ceases, we are able to see our own true nature with utmost clarity.
(Excerpted from *How to Practice the Buddhadharma*)

The practice of observing the mind is the essential task in cultivating the mind. Everything taught in the Mahāyāna scriptures never departs from prajñā, which is to say it never departs from mindful contemplation. Because in our daily life we cannot turn a single thought's light back to reflect upon our own nature, our deluded thoughts end up racing ceaselessly like a runaway horse. Now we use our own nature to shine upon our own mind — this is the fundamental method of severing the root when felling a tree. Therefore the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: “To be able to contemplate the mind's nature is called the highest samādhi.” The *Sūtra on Contemplation of the Mind Ground* likewise says: “If one can cultivate this profound and subtle contemplation, delusion, karma, and the fruit of suffering will have no way to arise.”

The method of observing the mind: at the very start, you must let go of all deluded and scattered thoughts at all times and in all places, giving no thought to right or wrong, good or evil, and directly, quietly watch your present thought in fine detail. At this moment you will only see thoughts coming and going in a flash, arising and ceasing like illusions. You must on no account discriminate or cling to them, nor drift along with them, nor deliberately try to dispel them, for deluded thoughts are in themselves empty and were never anything that could be dispelled. We need only observe them calmly and minutely: once a deluded thought is illuminated by the mind itself, it can immediately become still and motionless, until it naturally dissolves into formlessness. But at the outset one tends to forget easily, so one must practice often — at least several dozen times a day — and it will gradually ripen of itself.

Halfway through the contemplation, a single thought often rises with tremendous force and may linger three or four days without departing; this is precisely the seed of habitual tendency stirring within. At such a time simply keep observing and illuminating, pay it no heed, be firm in resolve, and endure it with bowed head, using the method of “neither grasping nor rejecting.” After long practice, you will come to feel that deluded thoughts no longer flow, the mind-ground is empty and pure, stillness and illumination are simultaneous, and the luminous light shines alone.

To put the principle of observing the mind briefly: the wisdom that observes is prajñā, and the object observed by that wisdom is ignorance. But ignorance arises only in dependence upon thusness (tathatā), and so to observe the deluded mind of ignorance is to observe the pure mind of one's own nature. In this way, steeping ignorance in prajñā is just like letting sunlight fall upon solid ice: shine upon it long enough, and there is none of it that will not melt away piece by piece and dissolve back into its own nature.

Furthermore, the prajñā that observes and illuminates is initial enlightenment, while the prajñā of true reality is original enlightenment. Through this initial enlightenment of turning the light back to reflect inward, delusion is gradually stilled and the true revealed. The stronger the power of observation, the fuller the power of concentration; when concentration and wisdom nourish each other, the initial and the original merge into one. Like a pearl that emits light and shines it back upon its own body, once all delusions are stilled, stillness and illumination appear directly before you. This is exactly the practice described in the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* as “perfectly illuminating the pure appearance of enlightenment.” Therefore the practice of observing the mind is called, in the *Sūtra on Contemplation of the Mind Ground*, “the Dharma-gate of sudden awakening that enters the stage of the Tathāgata.”

After seeing the nature, one's practice is by no means complete. It is like having mastered marksmanship: it is now that one must break the enemy. If one meets the enemy and does not resist, then the bandits run rampant and the world will never know a day of peace. Therefore, at this stage one must rely on the power of illuminating wisdom to sweep away habitual tendencies step by step, and one must use all human affairs to temper and polish oneself. For every affliction is a place for training the mind, and every difficulty a place for training wisdom and strength; moreover, it is only amid worldly toil and adversity that one can heighten one's vigilance and rouse one's resolve — as the ancients said: “Only when the mind is distressed and the thoughts obstructed does one rise to action!”

In the course of observing the mind, one must be resolute and determined, unceasingly strengthening oneself, and constantly struggle against one's own habitual tendencies. Views (the affliction of views) are attachment to self — dissolve them into emptiness; emotions (the affliction of thought) are self-love — turn away and loosen them. The harder something is to dissolve, the more one must dissolve it. Always go against oneself; only by enduring what obstructs you can you make progress.

When the contemplation becomes effective, midway there will inevitably arise the phenomenon of the mind becoming extraordinarily disordered: either desires burst forth wildly or the mind grows fretful and oppressed. This is because the many seeds of past habitual tendencies stored in the eighth consciousness are being stirred up by the pressure of the practice. This is precisely the moment of progress, so do not doubt it. Simply know that they are empty by nature, and neither grasp nor reject, dealing with them calmly and steadily. (The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* says: “When you know they are flowers in the sky, there is no more turning on the wheel.”) The more violently they churn, the more mud is removed; after hundreds and thousands of churnings up and down, one naturally realizes the state of unmoving.

The process of putting the Buddhadharma into practice is none other than the process of subduing and cutting off afflictions, delusions, and habitual tendencies. To whatever degree habitual tendencies are removed, to that same degree is the Buddha's knowledge and vision unfolded.

What are called habitual tendencies are, in origin, the illusory workings of one's own mind. They are of three natures — wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate — and are formed by the deluded mind's shadows of the six sense-objects being steeped and shaped again and again. Now that we wish to cut off afflictions and habitual tendencies, we must set to work on the afflictions and habitual tendencies themselves; avoiding them or suppressing them is of absolutely no use. Moreover, habitual tendencies generally come to light along with human affairs, and so we must use all favorable and adverse circumstances to temper ourselves: regard illness and pain as good medicine, regard calamity as liberation, and even “receive vicious abuse as if drinking sweet nectar, and meet with adversity as if gaining a rare treasure.” Testing the mind against every circumstance and enduring hardship with diligence is truly the crucial point in removing habitual tendencies.

After the Second Patriarch attained awakening, he concealed his light and mingled with the crowd, now entering the wine shops, now listening to street talk — this was precisely his practice of removing habitual tendencies. The habits we carry in daily life, whether good or bad, wholesome or unwholesome, so long as we cling to them and cannot easily dissolve them, are the very root of suffering and birth and death. We should therefore apply great diligence and great endurance, constantly battling our own habitual tendencies and training in the practice of non-dwelling and non-attachment. From small battles to great battles, from small victories to great victories, learning again and again, penetrating deeper and deeper — only thus does one take on the manner of a buddha or a patriarch. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: “By rightly contemplating all dharmas, the root of wisdom grows; valiant and diligent, one crushes all the māras; measureless wisdom, awe-inspiring light blazing forth.”

The principle can be awakened to all at once, but the practice must be cultivated step by step.” Removing habitual tendencies is certainly no simple matter. Moreover, in the course of practice, the deeper one's skill, the more habitual tendencies churn to the surface. They often come suddenly and rise abruptly; without long, painstaking effort at tempering, supervision, and care, they can never be dissolved at a stroke in a single flash of awareness. One must use all manner of skillful means to make them fall away — this is entirely a question of strength and practice.

To sum up, removing habitual tendencies passes through the following stages: ordinary people are beset by affliction and deluded thoughts all day long, mistaking the false for the true, and are forever falling into the labyrinth of their own subjective views without knowing it. Only when suffering makes them aware of it do they realize how harmful their deluded thoughts and habitual tendencies are, and then they are willing to cultivate the Buddhadharma as an antidote. But in the early stage of practice their state of mind is bound to be half-believing and half-doubting, now clear and now dim — understanding only, with no realization to confirm it. Speaking of the precepts, they cling to external forms; speaking of concentration, they grasp at rigid stillness; speaking of wisdom, they fall back on Chan rhetoric. When habitual tendencies arise, they still lack the strength to resist them — exactly the case of “present when talked about, absent when put to use.”

After concentrated cultivation of the Buddhadharma, and after hundreds and thousands of rounds of tempering and resistance, one's state of mind gradually opens and brightens, one's strength gradually becomes sufficient, and one is able to awaken to one's own original essence. At this point one knows that all right and wrong, favorable and adverse, beautiful and ugly, hateful and beloved, are nothing but the illusory discriminations of one's own mind, and one is able not to be carried along by them, and gradually to extinguish one's own habitual tendencies: from coarse and heavy to subtle and light; from long-lasting to short-lived; from thick to bland; from great matters to small matters; from forced to natural; from powerless to powerful; from deliberate to unconscious. In short, the root of habitual tendencies has been loosened, and no longer holds as it once did with stubborn clinging. Continuing thus to sweep away habitual tendencies with prajñā, the power of concentration and wisdom grows stronger day by day, becoming an overwhelming force that nothing can withstand. Toward one's own habitual tendencies one can now shine perfect illumination everywhere and awaken at every moment; one's own nature gradually becomes a single, seamless, perfectly bright whole — utterly still, without a single thought, yet so vividly alive as to be beyond conception. There is no need to strain at gathering the mind in, for naturally it does not scatter. When a habitual tendency arises, one turn and it is nowhere to be found, nothing one can grasp. Delusion cannot be grasped, and awakening cannot be felt. Neither moving nor still, neither ordinary nor holy, it transcends all thought and words — this is precisely what is meant by “perfect enlightenment.”

The cultivation of every Dharma-gate is inseparable from awareness and illumination. For when the mind meets its object, if there is no illumination there is no transformation; without transformation there is no emptiness; without emptiness there is no concentration; without concentration there is no wisdom. In the process of sweeping away habitual tendencies, the progress of the power of awareness and illumination may be divided into the following levels:
1. The mind arises first and awareness follows after, and it must be raised with all one's might;
2. Although awareness still follows the arising of the mind, it can be raised without much effort;
3. One can be aware the moment the mind arises, though there is still a slight gap of before and after;
4. When the mind arises, awareness arises at the same instant;
5. Awareness comes first and the mind-thought follows, though one still sometimes forgets to be aware;
6. Awareness can remain always in front, but one is still mindful of the awareness itself (the above are all within the realm of practice);
7. One is unaware of there being any illumination, yet has not departed from it; one clearly knows there are objects, yet there was never any obstruction;
8. One enters the state of constant stillness and constant illumination.
We may examine ourselves as to which stage we have actually reached.
